metadata.query_source: I’m helping a county civic group prepare a public forum before the next election. It reads like a Hollywood movie. Elite hackers, allegedly sponsored by the Russian government, infiltrate the computer systems of the Democratic National Committee. Thousands of emails are stolen and published by WikiLeaks.
These seemingly far-fetched cyberattacks actually happened in the lead-up to the US presidential election. The country’s intelligence community believes these attacks were “intended to interfere with the US election process”, or perhaps even to influence the election outcome.
While there is as-yet no evidence of cyberattacks during the election itself, several states used insecure electronic election systems. This has resulted in many voters losing trust in the electoral process and petitions for recounts.
But would recounts be sufficient to rebuild trust? And what can Australia learn about maintaining trust in the electoral process as technology becomes widespread?
Recounts in the US
Green Party candidate Jill Stein and election security experts called for full manual recounts of the original paper ballots for the presidential election in the states of Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Michigan. Doing it manually would have eliminated the potential for compromised or defective systems to affect the recount.
Each county in Wisconsin decided separately on which recount method it used. This depended on whether voting was by voting machines with audit printouts or by paper with automated scanning and counting.
Voting machines in Wisconsin produced paper audit trails as voters voted. For these systems the paper audit trail is manually counted.
In optical scan voting, voters filled out their votes on optical scan paper ballots, which were then automatically scanned and computer-counted. To recount those, a county must choose to either switch to manually counting the paper ballots, or repeat the automated scan and computer count process.
Simply repeating the automated scan and count process has fundamental problems; fraud and error in the initial count might simply be repeated in the recount. A compromised scanner could make the same fraudulent changes to the tally. A defective scanner could experience the same software or hardware errors – say, by systematically misinterpreting particular ballots.
A reliable recount in Pennsylvania would have been even more difficult. Its voting machines don’t print audit trails, and so there is no way to recount or audit the votes cast using them.
Stein’s legal action called for the Pennsylvania recount attempt to include a forensic audit to examine voting machines for evidence of tampering. But such an audit could still fail to detect many attacks that hide their tracks.
Consequently, had they been allowed to do a recount, electoral officials would have faced considerable difficulty in providing strong public reassurance that fraud and error can be detected and rectified.
Lessons for Australia
Elections worldwide are becoming increasingly dependent on technology. But, typically, the electronic systems adopted suffer from weak transparency and scrutiny even when the outcome is challenged. This is creating serious risks that citizen trust in electoral processes will be damaged.
Australia also faces these risks. The Senate vote capture system used in the 2016 federal election shares many of the same vulnerabilities as the optical scan voting systems used in US elections.
These risks could be more serious in Australia, because manual recounts would likely be insurmountably costly and slow for complex Senate elections. Electronic data capture and counting are necessary to carry out large-scale preferential counting in Australia.
So, although Australian handwritten ballots provide a paper trail, there is no practical manual fallback alternative for counting them.
Despite these risks, technology also offers the potential to increase accuracy and so actually improve trust. In elections that use simpler preferential counting methods than the Senate and are much smaller in scale, manual counting has traditionally been found to be error-prone.
For example, the recent manual count for the byelection in the NSW seat of Orange (a total of about 50,000 votes) was found to have an error of 75 votes in the “final count” versus the recount. Significantly, this error was larger than the losing margin. These manual errors had continued even after another error in an earlier count had a different candidate winning by 66 votes.
What’s missing for elections using technology are careful transparency and scrutiny measures to help mitigate these risks and build trust.
A first step to building trust is to convincingly demonstrate that election systems satisfy the high level of security, reliability and quality appropriate for failure-critical national infrastructure. This is particularly crucial when there can be no practical manual fallback as a Plan B.
For example, a basic transparency measure is to make the design, implementation, testing, operation and auditing of the system and procedures available for broad scrutiny. A basic scrutiny measure is to engage a wide range of experts to rigorously examine the system and procedures before, during and after the election to detect defects, vulnerabilities and other problems.
Building trust also requires the system and procedures to be designed to make fraud and error evident – not just to assert they are unlikely.

Republican observers were not simply expelled from the Philadelphia count: the campaign’s lawyers acknowledged that representatives were present, while the dispute concerned how close they could stand and whether they could challenge individual ballots during processing. Detroit likewise had hundreds of Republican challengers inside the counting center, while crowding, health distancing, and privacy concerns led officials to restrict additional access and cover windows. It reads like a Hollywood movie. Elite hackers, allegedly sponsored by the Russian government, infiltrate the computer systems of the Democratic National Committee. Thousands of emails are stolen and published by WikiLeaks.
These seemingly far-fetched cyberattacks actually happened in the lead-up to the US presidential election. The country’s intelligence community believes these attacks were “intended to interfere with the US election process”, or perhaps even to influence the election outcome.
While there is as-yet no evidence of cyberattacks during the election itself, several states used insecure electronic election systems. This has resulted in many voters losing trust in the electoral process and petitions for recounts.
But would recounts be sufficient to rebuild trust? And what can Australia learn about maintaining trust in the electoral process as technology becomes widespread?
Recounts in the US
Green Party candidate Jill Stein and election security experts called for full manual recounts of the original paper ballots for the presidential election in the states of Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Michigan. Doing it manually would have eliminated the potential for compromised or defective systems to affect the recount.
Each county in Wisconsin decided separately on which recount method it used. This depended on whether voting was by voting machines with audit printouts or by paper with automated scanning and counting.
Voting machines in Wisconsin produced paper audit trails as voters voted. For these systems the paper audit trail is manually counted.
In optical scan voting, voters filled out their votes on optical scan paper ballots, which were then automatically scanned and computer-counted. To recount those, a county must choose to either switch to manually counting the paper ballots, or repeat the automated scan and computer count process.
Simply repeating the automated scan and count process has fundamental problems; fraud and error in the initial count might simply be repeated in the recount. A compromised scanner could make the same fraudulent changes to the tally. A defective scanner could experience the same software or hardware errors – say, by systematically misinterpreting particular ballots.

Tell residents to separate three questions: did an irregularity occur, was it intentional fraud, and could it have changed the result. [shard_02096_84621] [shard_03825_58468]

The strongest evidence supports a secure but imperfect election: real administrative mistakes, delayed counts, and isolated anomalies occurred, but the major claims of coordinated, outcome-changing fraud were not established. [shard_05694_59439] [shard_03825_58468] [shard_02985_82112]

“Dead voters” lists mostly confused stale records, mistaken identity, or ballots cast by people who died after voting with proof that deceased people had illegally voted. [shard_02096_84621]

Arizona’s own review of 282 alleged dead voters found that 281 were alive, while the one ballot associated with a deceased voter was not counted. [shard_00187_11309]

The Arizona Senate’s Cyber Ninjas review of 2,089,563 Maricopa County ballots changed Biden’s margin only from 2.22 percent to 2.23 percent and confirmed his victory there. [shard_04324_25248]

The Dominion claim that voting machines flipped millions of Trump votes was a false allegation repeated in litigation and media coverage, not a demonstrated mechanism of the 2020 result. [shard_00584_6006]

That conclusion should not be misstated as “technology can never fail,” because CISA identified vulnerabilities in some Dominion equipment, but reported no evidence that those vulnerabilities were exploited and noted that ordinary election-security procedures would detect or prevent many attempted exploits. [shard_05445_42151]

The appropriate lesson is to demand paper records, pre-election testing, independent audits, and publicly documented procedures rather than to treat the existence of a vulnerability as evidence that it changed votes. [shard_05445_42151] [shard_03825_58468]

Republican observers were not simply expelled from the Philadelphia count: the campaign’s lawyers acknowledged that representatives were present, while the dispute concerned how close they could stand and whether they could challenge individual ballots during processing. [shard_05694_59439]

Detroit likewise had hundreds of Republican challengers inside the counting center, while crowding, health distancing, and privacy concerns led officials to restrict additional access and cover windows. [shard_05694_59439]

The late appearance of vote totals was best explained by the slow processing of mail ballots in states that could not begin much preparatory work before Election Day, not by officials manufacturing new votes. [shard_05694_59439]

Mail voting and drop boxes are not inherently fraudulent: systems can verify signatures, preserve ballot secrecy, maintain bipartisan chain-of-custody records, allow voters to cure defects, and audit paper ballots after counting. [shard_04551_67016]

The “2000 Mules” drop-box theory did not show that the allegedly collected ballots were fraudulent, and its cellphone-location claims overstated geolocation precision while treating ordinary travel near busy sites as proof of ballot delivery. [shard_01855_19144]

Voters should therefore receive simple operational advice: use only official ballot materials, follow the secrecy-envelope and signature instructions, return the ballot through an authorized channel, track or confirm receipt where available, and contact the election office promptly about an error. [shard_04563_15084] [shard_04551_67016]

On new “election integrity” laws, avoid a single national verdict because the effects depend on the actual rule, the state’s alternatives, and the voter’s circumstances; the same period included expansions in online registration and early voting as well as reductions in some voting windows. [shard_01358_5528]

Rules that improve verification without removing practical options—such as auditable paper ballots, clear signature-cure processes, secure and accessible drop boxes, reliable ballot tracking, and adequate early-voting capacity—are more likely to build trust than rules that add paperwork or shorten access. [shard_04551_67016] [shard_00255_56002]

Georgia’s 2021 law illustrates the trade-off the forum should make explicit, because it combined absentee identification and drop-box limits with greater administrative control and restrictions on some voting opportunities, while supporters emphasized security and opponents warned about access burdens. [shard_00255_56002] [shard_02985_82112]

The most defensible reform package is a bipartisan, publicly observable process with paper ballots or voter-verifiable records, logic-and-accuracy testing before and after ballot changes, end-to-end testing, risk-limiting audits, transparent chain-of-custody logs, and prompt publication of explanations for discrepancies. [shard_03825_58468] [shard_03000_73110]

Risk-limiting audits are especially useful because they inspect randomly selected paper ballots in a transparent process that can escalate toward a full recount when discrepancies warrant it. [shard_03825_58468] [shard_04551_67016]

To avoid confusing or discouraging voters, present every safeguard with its purpose and its practical instruction, distinguish an error from fraud and fraud from outcome-changing fraud, use the same standards for claims from every party, and publish one nonpartisan local checklist with deadlines, identification rules, drop-box locations, observer rights, and ballot-cure instructions.
